meta.title: Who really said "Wrong does not cease to be wrong because the majority share in it"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Credited to Leo Tolstoy’s A Confession — but the line is in neither of two English translations, nor anywhere else in his works. Origin undocumented.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Wrong does not cease to be wrong because the majority share in it'?
meta.ogDescription: Not in A Confession. Not in Tolstoy at all. We searched two translations of the named book and forty-five more of his works. No documented origin.

answer.label: Not Leo Tolstoy — an unsourced maxim
answer.authorDates: Origin undocumented · circulated under Tolstoy’s name
answer.sourceLine: Every popular posting names the same book — Tolstoy’s A Confession — and the sentence is not in it, in either of two independent English translations. A word-search across roughly thirty megabytes of Tolstoy in English turns up neither the sentence nor the phrases “majority share” and “cease to be wrong,” and no earlier speaker has been documented for the line either.
answer.confidenceText: Not found in the named source, or in any Tolstoy work searched; no alternative originator documented.

source.heading: The book everyone names, and what is actually in it

docMeta.dd: Aylmer Maude, A Confession and What I Believe (Oxford University Press, 1921); and My Confession, My Religion, The Gospel in Brief (Thomas Y. Crowell, New York, 1899)
Phrase absent from both. Neither translation contains the sentence, the words “majority share,” or the words “cease to be wrong.”
Absent from 45 further Tolstoy titles in English, from Chronicling America, and from Wikisource full text. No documented originator.

source.excerpt: Wrong does not cease to be wrong because the majority share in it.
trail: The claim is unusually specific and therefore testable: Goodreads ↗ attributes the line to “Leo Tolstoy, A Confession.” That book runs to sixteen short chapters and is freely available in full — Aylmer Maude’s translation is on Wikisource ↗.

Two independent English translations were searched end to end: Maude’s 1921 Oxford edition ↗ and the 1899 Crowell edition ↗. Neither contains the sentence, and neither contains the words “majority share” or the words “cease to be wrong.”

Widening the net changed nothing. Forty-five Tolstoy titles in English from Project Gutenberg ↗ — including The Kingdom of God Is Within You ↗, the work where such an argument would most plausibly sit — produced no match, and neither did a phrase search of the Library of Congress Chronicling America ↗ newspaper corpus.

Wikiquote’s Leo Tolstoy page ↗ keeps a sourced Confession (1882) section and does not include this line anywhere. It appears on Wikiquote only under the topic page Relativism ↗, cited as nothing more than “Leo Tolstoy, A Confession.”
source.excerptNote: Shown as it circulates. There is no fuller original context to give, because no original has been found — in Tolstoy or anywhere else.

sourceLink.text: A Confession — complete Maude translation at Wikisource

source.rightsNote: No rights status is asserted, because no source work has been identified. The wording cannot be traced to any published text by Tolstoy or anyone else, so there is no first-publication date on which to base a public-domain or in-copyright determination. Tolstoy’s own writings and the pre-1931 English translations checked here are separately in the public domain in the United States — but that says nothing about a sentence that is not in them.

author.name: Leo Tolstoy
author.heading: Leo Tolstoy — the name attached, not the source
author.bio: Count Lev Nikolayevich Tolstoy (9 September 1828 – 20 November 1910) wrote War and Peace and Anna Karenina, then spent his last three decades on religious and moral prose that attacked church, state and property alike. That second career — A Confession, The Kingdom of God Is Within You, the anti-war essays — is why moral one-liners drift onto his name so easily: he really did spend thirty years arguing that conscience outranks custom. He is listed here as the misattributed name, not as the author of this sentence — the wording does not appear in his work.

misattribution.heading: How the credit went wrong
misattribution.intro: This is an unusually well-behaved misattribution: it is not vague. Almost every posting supplies the same author and the same book, which is what makes it easy to disprove and hard to dislodge.

items.why: Goodreads ↗ carries it as “— Leo Tolstoy, A Confession,” and that pairing is repeated across the aggregator sites. The book is short and fully digitised. Neither Aylmer Maude’s 1921 translation ↗ nor the 1899 Thomas Y. Crowell translation ↗ contains the sentence, or the words “majority share,” or the words “cease to be wrong.”

items.scope: Where the citation likely propagated from
items.why: The line is absent from Wikiquote’s Leo Tolstoy page ↗, which does have a sourced Confession (1882) section. It survives only on the topic page Relativism ↗, where the whole citation reads “Leo Tolstoy, A Confession” — no translator, no edition, no page.

No earlier speaker or writer has been established. A phrase search of the Library of Congress Chronicling America ↗ newspaper archive returns nothing, and Quote Investigator ↗ has never published on it. Reassigning the line to a different famous name would repeat the original error.

misattribution.truthLine: The thought is old and the wording is not Tolstoy’s. The nearest documented ancestor — that a crowd cannot make a falsehood true — is far older than the Tolstoy credit: Quote Investigator traces “the united voice of myriads cannot lend the smallest foundation to falsehood” ↗ to Oliver Goldsmith’s The Vicar of Wakefield, 1766.

context.heading: Why this one sticks to Tolstoy
lead: The sentence is a good maxim wearing a borrowed coat. Its logic — that a headcount cannot convert a wrong into a right — is genuinely close to what Tolstoy spent his last thirty years arguing, which is precisely why nobody stops to check it. He did dismiss the crowd as an alibi: in Aylmer Maude’s 1911 collection of Tolstoy’s essays and letters ↗, the essay “Why Do Men Stupefy Themselves?” picks apart the excuse that people drink and smoke “because everybody does it,” and concludes something more powerful must be at work. Same instinct. Different sentence.

What makes the attribution collapse is the citation attached to it. The crowd-sourced version of this quote does not stop at “Tolstoy” — it names A Confession, a short, famous, fully digitised book. That specificity is checkable, and it does not survive the check. A quote that had merely floated free might still be a stray line from an untranslated letter; a quote pinned to the wrong page of the right author is a different animal.
detailsBody: A Confession, twice. The Aylmer Maude translation (Oxford University Press, 1921) and the earlier Thomas Y. Crowell translation (New York, 1899). Neither contains the phrase; neither contains “majority share” or “cease to be wrong.”

The wider corpus. Forty-five Tolstoy titles in English from Project Gutenberg — including The Kingdom of God Is Within You, What Is Art?, My Religion, What to Do?, Resurrection, War and Peace and Anna Karenina — plus Maude’s Essays and Letters, Recollections and Essays and The Slavery of Our Times from the Internet Archive. Not one of those texts contains the phrase, the words “majority share,” or the words “cease to be wrong.”
Print before the internet. A phrase search of the Library of Congress Chronicling America ↗ newspaper corpus returns no match for the phrase. Wikisource’s full-text index returns none either.

The specialists. Quote Investigator has published nothing on this line — its own site search for “cease to be wrong” returns “Nothing Found.” So there is no expert finding to defer to here, and none to contradict.
context.pull: A headcount cannot convert a wrong into a right — but a headcount of blog posts cannot convert a maxim into a quotation, either.
